questions.title: Git Branching Strategies
questions.question: What are the common Git branching strategies and which is best for a Java backend team?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Trunk-Based Development (TBD): short-lived branches, merge to main daily — modern CI/CD best practice
- Gitflow: long-lived develop, release, hotfix branches — complex, good for versioned software
- GitHub Flow: feature branches → main with PR review — simple, continuous deployment
- Feature flags: complement TBD — merge incomplete features behind a flag
- Release branches: for maintaining multiple versions (enterprise software)
- Most Java microservice teams use GitHub Flow or Trunk-Based Development
- Protection rules: require PR + review + passing CI before merge to main

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
For modern Java backend teams doing continuous deployment, GitHub Flow is the most practical approach. Developers create short-lived feature branches from main, implement the change, open a pull request for code review, and merge to main after CI passes and the review is approved. Main is always deployable. This keeps the workflow simple and reduces the merge conflict overhead that comes with longer-lived branches.

Trunk-Based Development takes this further — branches are even shorter-lived, often merged within a day or two. This requires feature flags to hide incomplete work in production. Teams doing TBD tend to ship faster and have fewer merge conflicts, but it requires a mature CI/CD pipeline and good feature flag management.

Gitflow is worth knowing because many companies use it, but it adds complexity — a long-lived develop branch that diverges from main, separate release branches, and hotfix branches. It makes sense for software with formal versioned releases, like a library or enterprise application, but it's overkill for a continuously deployed microservice.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## GitHub Flow

```bash
# 1. Create feature branch from main
git checkout main && git pull
git checkout -b feature/add-payment-service

# 2. Implement and commit regularly
git add -p  # stage changes interactively
git commit -m "feat(payments): add Stripe payment gateway integration"
git commit -m "test(payments): add integration tests for payment flow"

# 3. Push and open PR
git push -u origin feature/add-payment-service
# → Open PR on GitHub/GitLab

# 4. After review + CI passes → squash merge to main
git checkout main && git merge --squash feature/add-payment-service
git commit -m "feat(payments): add Stripe payment gateway integration (#123)"
git push

# 5. Deploy main automatically via CI/CD
# 6. Delete feature branch
git branch -d feature/add-payment-service
git push origin --delete feature/add-payment-service
```

## Gitflow (for versioned releases)

```
main     ──────────────────────────────── v1.0 ──────── v1.1
               ↑ merge                     ↑ merge
develop  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
               ↑ merge     ↑ merge
feature/A ─────────────────
feature/B          ─────────────────
           ↑ branch from develop

Hotfix: branch from main → merge to main AND develop
Release: branch from develop → merge to main AND develop
```

## Branch Protection Rules (GitHub)

```yaml
# GitHub branch protection for 'main':
require_pull_request_reviews:
  required_approving_review_count: 1
require_status_checks:
  strict: true  # must be up to date with main before merging
  contexts:
    - "CI / build-and-test"
    - "CI / integration-tests"
dismiss_stale_reviews: true
require_conversation_resolution: true
restrict_pushes: true  # no direct push to main
```

## Conventional Commits

```bash
# Structured commit messages enable automated changelogs and semantic versioning
git commit -m "feat(auth): add OAuth2 Google login"
git commit -m "fix(orders): prevent duplicate order creation on retry"
git commit -m "perf(cache): add Redis caching for product list"
git commit -m "refactor(db): extract database migrations to separate module"
git commit -m "docs(api): update OpenAPI spec for payments endpoint"
git commit -m "test(inventory): add unit tests for stock reservation"

# Breaking change (triggers major version bump)
git commit -m "feat(api)!: change order response format to include nested items

BREAKING CHANGE: order.products[] renamed to order.items[]"
```

speakable_v2.hook: For modern Java backend teams doing continuous deployment, GitHub Flow is the most practical approach.
speakable_v2.cap: It makes sense for software with formal versioned releases, like a library or enterprise application, but it's overkill for a continuously deployed microservice.

questions.title: Git Rebase vs Merge
questions.question: What is the difference between git rebase and git merge, and when should you use each?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Merge: creates a merge commit preserving full history — non-destructive
- Rebase: replays commits on top of another branch — linear history, rewrites commit SHAs
- Fast-forward merge: when no divergence — pointer just advances (no merge commit)
- Interactive rebase: squash, reorder, edit, drop commits before merging PR
- Golden rule: never rebase shared/public branches — rewrites history others have
- Rebase workflow: rebase local feature branch onto latest main before PR
- Squash merge: team gets linear main history without individual intermediate commits

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Merge preserves the full history of both branches and creates a merge commit to record where they joined. The history shows exactly what happened — which features were developed in parallel and when they were integrated. The downside is a messy history with many merge commits in a team with many concurrent feature branches.

Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch as if you had started your work from the latest commit. The result is a linear history that reads like a clear narrative of changes. The critical rule is never to rebase commits that you've already pushed and shared with others — rebasing rewrites commit SHAs, so if others have pulled your commits, their history will diverge.

In practice, I use rebase locally to incorporate the latest main into my feature branch before opening a PR — this resolves conflicts on my branch rather than in a merge commit. Then the team uses squash merge when merging PRs to main, which turns all my intermediate commits into one clean commit. This gives main a linear, readable history while preserving the full detail in the feature branch.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Merge vs Rebase Comparison

```
# Starting state:
main:    A ── B ── C
                    \
feature:             D ── E

# git merge main (from feature branch)
main:    A ── B ── C ────────── M  ← merge commit
                    \          /
feature:             D ── E ──
# History: shows parallel development — non-destructive

# git rebase main (from feature branch)
main:    A ── B ── C
                    \
feature:             D' ── E'  ← replayed on top of C, new SHAs
# History: looks like feature was built after C — linear
```

## Common Workflow

```bash
# Before opening a PR: update feature branch with latest main
git checkout feature/my-feature
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main  # replay my commits on top of latest main

# Resolve any conflicts during rebase
git add .
git rebase --continue  # continue after resolving
# or: git rebase --abort  # start over

git push --force-with-lease  # update remote (safe force push)
# --force-with-lease: fails if someone else pushed — safer than --force
```

## Interactive Rebase — Clean Up Before PR

```bash
# Squash last 3 commits into one before PR
git rebase -i HEAD~3

# Editor opens:
# pick a1b2c3 wip: add payment service
# pick d4e5f6 fix typo
# pick g7h8i9 add tests

# Change to:
# pick a1b2c3 feat(payments): add Stripe payment service
# squash d4e5f6 fix typo          ← squash into previous
# squash g7h8i9 add tests          ← squash into previous

# Result: one clean commit with a good message
```

## Squash Merge Strategy

```bash
# Merge PR as one commit onto main
git checkout main
git merge --squash feature/add-payment-service
git commit -m "feat(payments): add Stripe payment gateway (#42)"

# main gets a linear history:
# A ── B ── C ── feat(payments)   ← one commit for entire feature
# No merge commit, no intermediate WIP commits visible
```

speakable_v2.hook: Merge preserves the full history of both branches and creates a merge commit to record where they joined.
speakable_v2.cap: This gives main a linear, readable history while preserving the full detail in the feature branch.

questions.title: Resolving Git Conflicts and Cherry-Pick
questions.question: How do you resolve complex Git merge conflicts and use cherry-pick effectively?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Conflict: two branches modified same lines differently — Git can't auto-merge
- Markers: <<<<<<< HEAD, =======, >>>>>>> branch — mark the two conflicting versions
- Resolution: edit the file to the correct final state, then git add
- Diff tools: git mergetool, IDE integration (IntelliJ 3-way merge view)
- Cherry-pick: apply a specific commit from one branch to another
- Use cases: backport a bug fix to a release branch, pull a specific fix from main
- Conflicts during cherry-pick: same resolution process as merge
- git blame / git log -p: find who introduced a change and understand context

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Merge conflicts happen when two branches modify the same lines and Git can't determine which version to keep. Git marks the conflicting sections with <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers showing both versions. Your job is to edit the file to the correct final state — which might be one version, the other, or a combination — then mark it as resolved with git add.

For complex conflicts, a visual merge tool makes the process much clearer. IntelliJ's built-in three-pane merge view shows your version, the incoming version, and the current merged result side by side. You click on which hunks to accept from each side. This is far less error-prone than editing the raw conflict markers.

Cherry-pick applies a single commit from one branch to another. The most common use case is backporting a bug fix: you merged the fix to main, but the production version is a release branch. You cherry-pick the specific fix commit onto the release branch without bringing along everything else that has been merged to main since the release.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Resolving Merge Conflicts

```bash
# During merge or rebase, conflict appears
git merge feature/update-user-api
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/main/java/UserController.java

# View conflicted files
git status  # shows both modified: UserController.java

# In the file:
<<<<<<< HEAD (current branch — main)
    @GetMapping("/users/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDTO> getUser(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(userService.findById(id));
    }
=======
    @GetMapping("/users/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDTO> getUser(@PathVariable Long id,
                                            @RequestParam boolean includeOrders) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(userService.findById(id, includeOrders));
    }
>>>>>>> feature/update-user-api (incoming)

# Edit to correct final state (combine both changes):
    @GetMapping("/users/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<UserDTO> getUser(@PathVariable Long id,
                                            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "false") boolean includeOrders) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(userService.findById(id, includeOrders));
    }

# Mark resolved and continue
git add src/main/java/UserController.java
git merge --continue  # or git rebase --continue
```

## Cherry-Pick — Backport Bug Fix

```bash
# Scenario: fix was applied to main, need it on release/1.2 branch

# Find the commit SHA
git log --oneline main | grep "fix(orders)"
# a1b2c3d fix(orders): prevent negative stock on concurrent requests

# Cherry-pick to release branch
git checkout release/1.2
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d

# Cherry-pick multiple commits
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d b2c3d4e

# Cherry-pick a range (exclusive..inclusive)
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d..f6g7h8i
```

## Useful Diagnostic Commands

```bash
# Who last modified a line (useful for understanding conflicts)
git blame src/main/java/UserService.java
# Shows: commit SHA, author, date, line content

# What changed in a specific commit
git show a1b2c3d

# History of changes to a specific file
git log --follow -p src/main/java/UserService.java

# Find when a bug was introduced
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD              # current commit is broken
git bisect good v1.2.0          # this version was working
# Git binary searches — test each suggested commit
git bisect good   # or: git bisect bad
# Git finds the exact commit that introduced the bug
```

speakable_v2.hook: Merge conflicts happen when two branches modify the same lines and Git can't determine which version to keep.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: You cherry-pick the specific fix commit onto the release branch without bringing along everything else that has been merged to main since the release.

questions.title: Effective Pull Request Practices
questions.question: What makes a good pull request and how do you conduct effective code reviews?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Small PRs: easier to review, less risk, faster to merge — aim for < 400 lines changed
- Description: what, why, and how — not just what the code does
- Linked issue: PR should reference the ticket/issue it addresses
- CI must pass before review: don't ask for review if tests are failing
- Review focus: logic correctness, security, performance, design — not style (automated linters)
- Non-blocking comments: prefix with 'nit:' or 'optional:' for minor suggestions
- Draft PRs: for early feedback before work is complete
- CODEOWNERS: auto-assign reviewers based on file paths

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A good pull request is small and focused. A PR that changes 2,000 lines of code across 30 files is nearly impossible to review effectively — reviewers get fatigued and miss issues. Aim for one logical change per PR, ideally under 400 lines changed. If a feature requires many changes, break it into a series of smaller PRs that can be reviewed and merged sequentially.

The PR description matters as much as the code. Include what the change does, why it's needed — link the ticket — and any important implementation decisions you made and why. If you considered alternative approaches and chose against them, say so. Reviewers shouldn't have to guess your intent.

As a reviewer, focus on logic, security, and design — not formatting and style. Linters handle style automatically. Ask questions rather than making demands when you're unsure — you might be missing context. Distinguish blocking issues from optional suggestions by prefixing minor comments with 'nit:' so the author knows what's required versus what's just an idea.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## PR Description Template

```markdown
## What
Add rate limiting to the public API endpoints using Redis sliding window counter.

## Why
We were getting abused by scrapers causing increased infrastructure costs.
Fixes: #247

## How
- Added `RateLimitingFilter` that runs before authentication
- Uses Redis sorted set per IP to track requests in a 1-minute sliding window
- Returns 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After header when limit exceeded
- Limit: 100 requests/min per IP (configurable via application.yml)

## Testing
- Unit tests: `RateLimitingFilterTest`
- Manual test: `curl` the endpoint 101 times to verify 429 response
- Load test: no performance impact below rate limit threshold

## Notes
- Excluded /actuator/health from rate limiting
- Rate limits are per-IP — logged-in users get same treatment (future: per-user limits)
```

## CODEOWNERS File

```
# .github/CODEOWNERS
# Global: any change requires review from team lead
*                       @team-lead

# Security changes: require security team review
/src/**/security/       @security-team
/src/**/auth/           @security-team

# Database migrations: require DBA review
/src/main/resources/db/ @dba-team

# Infrastructure: require DevOps review
/docker-compose*.yml    @devops-team
/.github/workflows/     @devops-team
```

## GitHub Actions: PR Quality Gates

```yaml
# .github/workflows/pr-checks.yml
name: PR Quality Checks
on: [pull_request]

jobs:
  lint-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { java-version: '21', distribution: 'temurin' }

      - name: Check code style
        run: mvn checkstyle:check

      - name: Run tests
        run: mvn test

      - name: Check test coverage
        run: mvn jacoco:report jacoco:check
        # Fails if coverage drops below configured threshold

      - name: Security scan
        run: mvn org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check
```

speakable_v2.hook: A good pull request is small and focused.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Distinguish blocking issues from optional suggestions by prefixing minor comments with 'nit:' so the author knows what's required versus what's just an idea.

questions.title: Git Stash, Reset and Recovery
questions.question: How do you use git stash, reset, and reflog to manage and recover from mistakes?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- git stash: temporarily shelve uncommitted changes
- git stash pop vs git stash apply: pop removes from stash, apply keeps it
- git reset --soft: undo commits, keep changes staged
- git reset --mixed (default): undo commits, keep changes unstaged
- git reset --hard: undo commits AND discard changes — dangerous, irreversible for local
- git reflog: safety net — records all HEAD movements including 'lost' commits
- git revert: safe undo for shared branches — creates new commit reversing changes
- git restore vs git checkout: modern commands for discarding file changes

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Git stash is for when you need to switch contexts quickly — you have unfinished work on a feature branch but an urgent bug needs your attention on main. Stash saves your changes, you switch branches, fix the bug, then come back and pop the stash to restore where you left off. You can even stash multiple sets of work and name them for clarity.

Git reset is for undoing commits. The three modes control what happens to the changes in those commits: soft keeps them staged, mixed keeps them but unstaged, and hard discards them entirely. Hard reset is the dangerous one — only use it for local commits you definitely don't want, never on commits you've pushed to a shared branch.

Git reflog is the ultimate safety net. It records every movement of HEAD for 90 days, including commits you've reset away or branches you've deleted. If you accidentally ran a hard reset and lost commits, reflog shows you the SHA of where you were before and you can recover it with git checkout or git reset.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Git Stash

```bash
# Stash uncommitted changes (tracked files)
git stash
git stash push -m "wip: payment service half done"
git stash push -u -m "wip: with new untracked files"  # -u includes untracked

# List stashes
git stash list
# stash@{0}: On feature/payments: wip: payment service half done
# stash@{1}: On feature/auth: wip: login flow

# Restore latest stash
git stash pop           # apply and remove from stash list
git stash apply         # apply but keep in stash list
git stash apply stash@{1}  # apply specific stash

# Discard a stash
git stash drop stash@{0}
git stash clear  # remove all stashes
```

## Git Reset

```bash
# Undo last commit, keep changes staged (to edit and recommit)
git reset --soft HEAD~1

# Undo last commit, keep changes but unstaged (default)
git reset HEAD~1

# Undo last commit, DISCARD changes (local only!)
git reset --hard HEAD~1

# Unstage a file (don't undo the change, just unstage)
git restore --staged src/PaymentService.java  # modern
git reset HEAD src/PaymentService.java        # old way

# Discard changes to a file (revert to last commit)
git restore src/PaymentService.java
```

## Git Reflog — Recovery

```bash
# Show all recent HEAD movements
git reflog
# a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
# f4e5d6c HEAD@{1}: commit: feat(payments): add Stripe integration
# b7c8d9e HEAD@{2}: commit: test(payments): add unit tests
# a0b1c2d HEAD@{3}: commit: feat(payments): initial structure

# Oops! Hard reset deleted 3 commits
# Recover: reset back to where you were
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}  # or use the SHA directly
git reset --hard f4e5d6c

# Or create a new branch at the lost commit
git checkout -b recovery-branch f4e5d6c
```

## git revert — Safe Undo for Shared Branches

```bash
# NEVER reset shared branches — creates diverging history
# Instead: revert creates a NEW commit that undoes the change
git revert a1b2c3d  # creates commit: "Revert 'feat(payments): add Stripe'"
git push  # safe — no history rewrite

# Revert multiple commits
git revert a1b2c3d b2c3d4e  # two separate revert commits
git revert a1b2c3d..f6g7h8i  # revert a range
```

speakable_v2.hook: Git stash is for when you need to switch contexts quickly — you have unfinished work on a feature branch but an urgent bug needs your attention on main.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: If you accidentally ran a hard reset and lost commits, reflog shows you the SHA of where you were before and you can recover it with git checkout or git reset.

questions.title: Git in CI/CD — Trunk-Based Development
questions.question: What is trunk-based development and how does it enable continuous deployment?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Trunk-Based Development: short-lived feature branches, merge to main multiple times per day
- Feature flags: merge incomplete features behind a flag — trunk stays deployable
- Continuous Integration: every merge to main triggers full build + test pipeline
- Continuous Deployment: passing CI pipeline automatically deploys to production
- Branch lifetime: hours to 2 days — not weeks
- Benefits: fewer merge conflicts, faster feedback, smaller deployments, less risk
- Requires: fast test suite, automated deployment, feature flags, good monitoring
- LaunchDarkly / Unleash: feature flag services for Java

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Trunk-Based Development means every developer works close to main. Feature branches exist for a few hours to a couple of days at most. You integrate small changes frequently rather than large changes infrequently. This is the foundation of Continuous Deployment.

The challenge is: how do you merge incomplete features? The answer is feature flags. You ship the code but hide the new feature behind a flag that's off in production. The code is in production, tested by CI, but users don't see it until you flip the flag. When the feature is complete and tested, you enable it — often with a gradual rollout — and eventually remove the flag.

Short-lived branches dramatically reduce merge conflicts. If you've been working on a branch for 2 weeks and 20 other developers have been merging to main daily, you have a massive reconciliation problem. If your branch is 6 hours old, the delta is small and conflicts are rare.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Feature Flag with Unleash

```java
// pom.xml
// io.getunleash:unleash-client-java

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private final Unleash unleash;

    public PaymentResult processPayment(PaymentRequest request) {
        // Feature flag: new Stripe SDK vs old one
        if (unleash.isEnabled("payments.new-stripe-sdk",
                UnleashContext.builder().userId(request.getUserId()).build())) {
            return newStripeIntegration.process(request);
        } else {
            return legacyStripeIntegration.process(request);
        }
    }
}

// application.yml
unleash:
  app-name: payment-service
  instance-id: ${HOSTNAME:local}
  unleash-api: https://unleash.internal.company.com/api
  api-token: ${UNLEASH_TOKEN}
```

## CI/CD Pipeline for TBD

```yaml
# .github/workflows/main.yml
name: CI/CD Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { java-version: '21', distribution: 'temurin' }
      - run: mvn verify
        # Runs: compile + unit tests + integration tests + coverage check

  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'  # only deploy from main
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to production
        run: |
          # Build Docker image
          docker build -t my-app:${{ github.sha }} .
          # Push to ECR
          # Update ECS service
        # Full automated deployment — no manual approval for small changes
```

## TBD vs Gitflow Trade-offs

```
Trunk-Based Development:
  ✅ Fewer merge conflicts
  ✅ Faster feedback on integration issues
  ✅ Smaller, less risky deployments
  ✅ Enables Continuous Deployment
  ❌ Requires mature CI/CD pipeline
  ❌ Requires feature flags
  ❌ Requires good test coverage

Gitflow:
  ✅ Clear release gates
  ✅ Easier to understand for less mature teams
  ✅ Good for multiple versions in production
  ❌ Long-lived branches → merge conflicts
  ❌ Slower feedback
  ❌ Larger, riskier deployments
```

speakable_v2.hook: Trunk-Based Development means every developer works close to main.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: If your branch is 6 hours old, the delta is small and conflicts are rare.
